newsitem.title: UK: Dresdner Bank seeks to become a Euromarket force.
newsitem.headline: Dresdner Bank seeks to become a Euromarket force.

text.p: Dresdner Bank's move to shift its Eurobond operations to London to drum up more multi-currency business will help it gain ground on rival banks in the race to attract bond deals, traders said on Tuesday.

Dresdner Kleinwort Benson was 19th on the bookrunner league table at the end of the third quarter this year, with around $9.3 billion equivalent under its belt or 1.83 percent of the market share, Capital DATA Bondware showed.
Last year, the bank came three notches higher in 16th place constituting $10.40 billion worth of bonds, a 2.24 percent market share.
Dresdner said it would buy a team of around 17 Eurobond experts by taking over the London-based boutique Luthy Baillie Dowsett & Pethick.
This would beef up Dresdner Kleinwort Benson's currently thin Eurodollar activity, particularly with the respected Peter Luthy on board, primary market players said.
Luthy previously worked with Dresdner board member Hans-Georg Hoffman at Lehman Brothers and some dealers said the move may have been tied to their working relationship.
"Kleinwort is a very conservative player in the market so Luthy Bailly will take them into areas they have not got the expertise to cover," a Eurobond analyst said.

Another syndicate official said: "Luthy Baillie is a very experienced operation and there is no question bond market expertise in the legal, accounting, finance and corporate side is concentrated in London."
But the buying of the boutique raised doubts about the muscle power of Dresdner's Kleinwort Benson in the Euromarket.

Some traders said last week's Eurobond launched for Dresdner Finance BV -- a 150 million stg December 2001 offering -- reflected a lack of capability as BZW was invited as joint lead manager with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"If you can't even bring a small bond for your own name you must be struggling," one trader said.

Rival London bankers also doubted Dresdner's strategy and said the timing was surprising given that European economic and monetary union (EMU) was little more than two years away. Britain is considered one of the outsiders in terms of EMU, and many firms are casting their visions more towards the Continent.

"What they are doing is curious...I would have thought that Dresdner would have been better off going their own way in the same way that Commerzbank and WestLB have done, that is independently recruiting more staff."
Some also criticised the strategic fit with Luthy Baillie.

"They (Luthy Baillie) have specialised in finding pockets of demand for banks who cannot sell left-over paper. But now that they've lost their independence, the street (institutions) won't show them any business at all," one rival banker in London said.
